extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, students of poetry, and readers interested in poetic craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating or producing high-quality poetry: focuses on imagery, diction, thought, characterization, and the relation between poetic language and life (with comparisons between Renaissance and modern practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery moulded to circumstances, passion, or character
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagery becomes more characteristic of poetic genius when it 'moulds and colours itself to the circumstances, passion, or character, present and foremost in the mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer images that grow out of the situation and the speaker's or character's emotion rather than generic ornament. Examples cited: Lear, Othello, and Sonnet 98 ('Drawn after you, you pattern of all those'). Anti-pattern: picturesque but irrelevant images that do not reflect the present passion or character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery supplying succession with simultaneous feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagery should give the liveliest image of succession while conveying a feeling of simultaneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use compressed, vivid images that suggest motion and sequence yet feel immediate (example lines: 'With this, he breaketh from the sweet embrace... homeward through the dark laund runs apace' and the quatrain 'Look! how a bright star shooteth from the sky, So glides he in the night from Venus’ eye.'). This creates a sense of action unfolding and present sensation at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and energy of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Depth and energy of thought are indispensable; 'No man was ever yet a great poet, without being at the same time a profound philosopher.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should reflect a wide range of human knowledge, thought, passions, and language. Intellectual energy must balance creative power—without this depth, poetic brilliance will be transitory. Example: Shakespeare combines imagery with profound reflection; poetry is 'the blossom and the fragrancy of all human knowledge.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of creative power and intellectual energy
rubrics_metrics.description: The creative (imaginative) power and intellectual energy should wrestle and then be reconciled so each tempers the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a working tension between imagination and thought: where they initially conflict they should ultimately blend into a single voice (metaphor: two rapid streams finding a wider channel and flowing as one). Anti-pattern: imagination without intellectual grounding or thought without imagistic vivacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Studied knowledge and patient meditation
rubrics_metrics.description: Great poetic power arises not from passive inspiration alone but from study, meditation, and minute understanding: 'first studied patiently, meditated deeply, understood minutely, till knowledge... wedded itself to his habitual feelings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value persistent learning and deliberate craft. The poet is not merely an automaton of genius but a worker who forms intuitive knowledge through practice and study (Shakespeare portrayed as having acquired knowledge until intuitive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominion/mastery over language
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet should possess 'perfect dominion, often domination, over the whole world of language.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a wide, precise vocabulary and the power to control diction so that language serves thought and feeling rather than being a constraint. Anti-patterns: careless diction or reliance on fashionably obscure or overworn phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility while retaining individual unity
rubrics_metrics.description: A great poet may 'become all things, yet for ever remaining himself'—able to embody many characters/forms while preserving a singular poetic identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate the ability to render diverse personae and modes convincingly, yet maintain a consistent artistic center. Contrast modes like Shakespeare (Protean) and Milton (attracts forms to his ideal) to understand different successful strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of older polish with modern depth and novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal poet would combine the 'high finish, the appropriateness, the facility, the delicate proportion, and ... omnipresent grace' of fifteenth/sixteenth-century masters with the 'keener interest, deeper pathos, manlier reflection, and the fresher and more various imagery' of modern poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek technical finish (polish of diction, metrical subtlety) together with stronger emotional interest and conceptual depth. This is an explicit prescription: novelty of thought and feeling should not sacrifice craft, nor should craft suppress genuine passion and reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate specificity vs general imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between the older poets' general imagery (sun, moon, flowers—shared, shaped materials) and modern poets' tendency toward specific, portrait-like images; both approaches have value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specificity to arrest interest and individuation, but remember the older practice valued superior excellence in treating common subjects. The suggested best practice is a balanced approach—specific, striking images handled with polished technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate metrical and rhythmic construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Meter and movement should arise from intelligent purpose not mere convenience or mechanical adoption—avoid measures with overpowering mechanical tunes that compel the reader's voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose metre with conscious variation and purpose; avoid adopting a single mechanical couplet or stanzaic 'movement' that makes diction serve only rhythm. Anti-pattern: stanza/couplet forms that produce accidental differences and distract from meaning (example critique of some modern measures as 'galloping over a paved road in a German stage-waggon without springs').

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity and guardianship of the native tongue
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets should guard the purity of their native language with jealous care (citing Dante's De la volgare Eloquenza); language is 'the armoury of the human mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid fashionable, obscure, or meretricious diction. Favor clear, genuine mother-English and resist contaminating poetic language with gratuitous learned phrases or artificially affected expressions. Editorial principle: protect clarity and expressive power of native diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as essentially ideal and generic
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry, 'as poetry, is essentially ideal, that it avoids and excludes all accident; that its apparent individualities ... must be representative of a class.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters in poetry should embody generic, class-representative attributes rather than eccentricities of a single individual. The poetic person must be clothed with common attributes of the class that make them typical and useful for poetic purpose. Anti-pattern: undue emphasis on accidental individual detail that undermines the poem's representative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate selection and framing of character-voice
rubrics_metrics.description: When using a narrator or a character's voice (e.g., rustic or illiterate speakers), the poet must take care to preclude unintended impressions by providing adequate framing or introductory material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to introduce or frame a speaker can cause passages to 'sink' and jar the reader (example: The Thorn's need for an introductory poem; The Idiot Boy's risk of recalling 'disgusting images' of morbid idiocy). Provide context so that persona-language is interpreted as poetic act, not accidental coarseness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not uncritically adopt rustic/colloquial language as universal poetic medium
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that the 'real language of men' (especially low and rustic life) should be the medium of poetry is limited: rustic speech only applies to certain classes of poetry and requires prior cultivation/adjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about wholesale transfer of rustic dialect into poetry. Rustic language purified of provincialism still differs by county/village and lacks the conceptual vocabulary for abstract reflection; poets should adapt and sometimes elevate colloquial speech rather than copy it verbatim. Anti-pattern: treating 'real' (in the sense of merely conversational) language as a one-size-fits-all poetic diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocabulary and prior store of language required for expression under passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Passion does not create words; the nature of a person's language when excited depends on the 'number and quality' of general truths, conceptions, images, and words previously stored in the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a rich stock of ideas and words because intense feeling mobilizes what is already available; do not rely on emotion alone to produce apt diction. Practical implication: read and learn to expand the expressive resources available in moments of poetic excitement.
